source_refs.note: Book p. 99: 6.5 Geometric Progression, definition, term labels, r = a_n / a_(n-1) (text before 6.5.1)

blocks.text: A geometric progression or geometric sequence is a sequence in which each term after the first is found by multiplying the previous term by a nonzero constant \(r\) called the common ratio.

blocks.title: Teaching note

blocks.text:
Like arithmetic progression, we can label the terms of a geometric sequence as \(a_1, a_2, a_3\) and so on, \(a_1 \ne 0\). The \(n^{\text{th}}\) term is \(a_n\) and the previous term is \(a_{n-1}\). So,
\[a_n = r(a_{n-1})\]
Thus,

blocks.text_alt: r equals a n over a n minus 1

blocks.text: That is, the common ratio can be found by dividing any term by its previous term.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why must \(a_1 \ne 0\) and \(r \ne 0\)? If either were 0, every term after the first would be 0, and the ratio \(\frac{a_n}{a_{n-1}}\) would mean dividing by 0, which is not defined. So no term of a G.P. is ever zero.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text:
To test whether a sequence is a G.P., divide each term by the one before it. If all the ratios are equal, it is a G.P. and that common value is \(r\).
\(5, 10, 20, 40\): \(\frac{10}{5} = \frac{20}{10} = \frac{40}{20} = 2\), so it is a G.P. with \(r = 2\).
\(1, 2, 4, 7\): the ratios are \(2, 2, \frac{7}{4}\), not all equal, so it is not a G.P.
Always divide a term by the term before it (\(\frac{a_2}{a_1}\)), not the other way round.

blocks.caption: Arithmetic progression and geometric progression compared
rows: \(d\) may be any real number, also 0

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. G.P.: each term after the first = previous term \(\times r\), where \(r\) is a non-zero constant (the common ratio).
2. \(a_1 \ne 0\); \(a_n = r(a_{n-1})\).
3. \(r = \frac{a_n}{a_{n-1}}\): divide any term by its previous term.
4. A sequence is a G.P. only if all these ratios are equal.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Dividing the wrong way round: for \(16, 8, 4\), \(r = \frac{8}{16} = \frac{1}{2}\), not 2.
2. Checking only the first ratio: \(1, 2, 4, 7\) starts like a G.P. but is not one.
3. Subtracting instead of dividing: the difference is used for an A.P., the ratio for a G.P.
